title: Indian Americans Back Democrats by 3-to-1 Margin Ahead of 2026 Midterms, New Survey Finds
excerpt: The 2026 Asian American Voter Survey shows 66% of Indian Americans support Democratic congressional candidates, with 74% viewing Trump unfavorably.
body:
• Sixty-six percent of Indian-American registered voters back Democratic candidates for both the Senate and House, compared to 22% and 18% for Republicans respectively, according to the 2026 Asian American Voter Survey.
  • Ninety-two percent of Indian-American registered voters plan to vote in the November midterms, with 43% saying they are more enthusiastic than usual — the highest enthusiasm increase among major Asian ethnic groups surveyed.
  • Seventy-four percent of Indian Americans view President Trump unfavorably, including 56% who hold a very unfavorable opinion.
  • Cost of living and inflation dominate voter concerns across the broader Asian-American electorate, with 90% calling it very or extremely important.

A Community Leans Left — Decisively

Indian-American voters are heading into the 2026 midterm elections with unusually high enthusiasm and a commanding preference for Democratic candidates, according to a national survey released this week by Asian and Pacific Islander American Vote (APIAVote) and AAPI Data.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2094605684574978248

The survey, conducted between June 3 and July 27 among 2,066 registered voters — including 242 Indian Americans — found that 66 percent of Indian-American voters support Democratic candidates in both Senate and House races. Republican support stood at 22 percent for Senate races and 18 percent for House contests. Seven to nine percent favored another party.

Among those with a House preference, 60 percent said they strongly supported their chosen candidate, signaling depth of commitment rather than soft partisan leaning.

Sky-High Turnout Intent

Indian Americans reported the strongest voting enthusiasm of any major Asian ethnic group surveyed. Ninety-two percent of registered voters said they planned to cast a ballot in November — 74 percent "absolutely certain" and another 23 percent "fairly certain."

Forty-three percent described themselves as more enthusiastic about voting than usual, against 22 percent who were less enthusiastic and 32 percent who said their interest was about the same. The community's turnout projections outpace the broader Asian-American electorate, where 90 percent of registered voters said they planned to participate, up from 84 percent in 2022 and 86 percent in 2018.

Deep Disapproval of Trump

The survey found strong negative sentiment toward President Donald Trump among Indian-American voters. Seventy-four percent viewed him unfavorably — including 56 percent who held a "very unfavorable" opinion. Only 20 percent viewed him favorably, with just 7 percent describing their view as "very favorable."

These numbers align with earlier findings from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, whose 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey — a separate poll of 1,000 adults conducted late last year — found roughly seven in ten disapproving of Trump's overall job performance, with majorities rejecting his handling of immigration and the economy.

"Indian Americans are not abandoning the left, but they are signaling that their support cannot be assumed."

— Carnegie Endowment 2026 Survey authors

Nuances Beneath the Headline Numbers

Despite the strong Democratic lean, the party has not fully recovered its 2020 dominance among Indian Americans. The Carnegie survey found Democratic party identification slipped from 52 percent in 2020 to 46 percent in 2026, with nearly one-third now identifying as independents. Feeling-thermometer ratings of the Democratic Party cooled from 75 out of 100 in 2020 to 69 in 2026.

The Republican share, meanwhile, has held relatively steady. Indian American Republicans rated their party at 72 across survey waves, reflecting firmer partisan intensity on the right.

Inflation and cost of living are the dominant concerns. Across the broader AAPI electorate, 90 percent called it very or extremely important in determining their vote. Immigration registered as important but not decisive; foreign policy — including U.S.-India relations — barely factored into vote calculations.

What It Means for November

With an estimated 16 million Asian-American and Pacific Islander citizens eligible to vote in 2026 — including 1.6 million newly eligible since 2022 — the community's political weight is growing. Indian Americans, among the most affluent and fastest-growing ethnic groups in the United States, punch above their population share in fundraising and civic engagement: three-quarters said they had discussed politics with family or friends in the past year, and roughly one in five had attended a protest, rally, or local government meeting.

Both parties face a calculus. Democrats hold a commanding lead but cannot assume the community's loyalty. Republicans, despite deep Trump disapproval, could chip away at the growing independent bloc if they address economic concerns without the baggage of policies Indian Americans oppose — particularly on immigration, minority tolerance, and abortion rights.
nri_angle: Indian-American voters are poised to play an outsized role in the 2026 midterms, with high enthusiasm and strong Democratic preference driven partly by concerns over anti-Indian rhetoric and immigration policies.
author: Diaspora Desk
